Generally, it is highly discouraged for a couples counselor to also act as the individual therapist for one of the partners. Doing so creates a conflict of interest that can compromise the therapist's neutrality and make the other partner feel alienated. Because the primary "client" in couples therapy is the relationship itself, ethical guidelines typically recommend having separate therapists for individual and couples work.

If a therapist learns about infidelity during a one-on-one session, how they handle it depends on their disclosure policy, usually established at the start of treatment. Many couples counselors have a strict "no secrets" policy because keeping major secrets undermines the therapy. In this scenario, the counselor would typically encourage the individual to share the truth with their spouse. If the person refuses, the therapist cannot simply break confidentiality to tell the spouse. Instead, they would likely have to terminate the couples counseling, as they cannot ethically continue treating the relationship while holding such a significant secret.
